qiviut.origin: Qiviut is the fine underwool of the muskox, Ovibos moschatus, an Arctic ungulate of northern North America and Greenland; wild muskoxen are also studied in Norway. Supply comes from two channels: combing of farmed animals, as documented at the Musk Ox Farm in Palmer, Alaska, and fiber recovered from hides of wild muskoxen taken in subsistence, sport or commercial harvests, for example on Banks Island in the Canadian Arctic. Muskoxen have the lowest genome-wide heterozygosity reported among ungulates, and climate-linked disease is a growing conservation concern.
qiviut.structure: Muskox fleece combines long guard hair with a dense, downy undercoat, the qiviut. Measurements of fleece from 299 wild Banks Island hides found mean qiviut diameters of about 17.5 microns in adult females and 18.2 microns in adult males, with yearling qiviut about 1.7 microns finer, and diameter variability decreasing with age. Scoured yield averaged 93.3%, so relatively little mass is lost in cleaning. Qiviut is keratin with a scaled cuticle, and because cortisol and trace elements are deposited during growth, each fiber also records the animal's physiology.
qiviut.process: Qiviut grows seasonally; in captive trials hair growth was maximal in summer and absent in winter, and the fiber is later shed. On farms, loosening underwool is combed out by hand during the shed, which yields fiber mixed with some guard hair; from harvested animals, fleece can be recovered from hides. In both cases guard hair must be removed by hand picking or mechanical dehairing, and the down is then gently washed, carded and spun, often into light lace-weight yarn.
qiviut.performance: Qiviut is light and insulating, with the hygroscopic, self-extinguishing behavior and acid-dye affinity of keratin, and it is often left in its natural color. Its fine and fairly uniform diameter gives a soft handle, but lace structures and light yarns are delicate: they abrade, and they felt under agitation, heat and moisture. As with all protein fibers, clothes moth and carpet beetle larvae are a storage risk.
qiviut.identify: Burn tests (indicative only, and to be done with care) show ordinary keratin behavior. Microscopy of diameter distribution, scale pattern and guard-hair content, compared with published diameters for wild qiviut, can screen claims but cannot prove species. Peptide mass spectrometry or DNA testing against authenticated muskox reference fiber would be the stronger route. Blends should state percentages, since a product marketed with the word qiviut may contain only a small share.
qiviut.labeling: Qiviut is not a specialty fiber under the US Wool Products Labeling Act. Under 16 CFR 303.6, hair of other animals may be disclosed with the animal's name and the word hair, fiber or blend when present at 5% or more, or as fur fiber; whether the Inuktitut word qiviut alone meets the animal-name rule is not settled here, so adding muskox is the cautious choice. In the EU, qiviut is not among the named fine hairs in Annex I of Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011 and falls in the animal hair category, where the animal may be named.
qiviut.past: Muskoxen are harvested by subsistence and sport hunters in Nunavut and the Northwest Territories, and in 2001 researchers responding to rising commercial interest applied wool and cashmere measurement standards to describe qiviut from a Banks Island harvest. The Palmer farm offers one documented model of husbandry and hand combing, while wild harvests supply another stream. Qiviut now also serves science: hair cortisol is validated as a measure of stress, and element profiles of qiviut from 11 populations across North America and Greenland track population trends in a rapidly warming Arctic.
facts: maximal in summer, none observed in winter (captive trial)

hemp.origin: Industrial hemp is Cannabis sativa L. grown for stem fiber, the woody inner core called hurd, and seed. In US federal law, the Agriculture Improvement Act of 2018 defines hemp as Cannabis sativa L. and any part of it with a delta-9 tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) concentration of not more than 0.3% on a dry weight basis (7 U.S.C. 1639o). China has long been the leading producer of hemp fiber. In Europe, France has long been among the main producers, and EU farm-support rules also use a 0.3% THC limit.
hemp.structure: Hemp bast fibers form bundles in the outer stem around a lignified woody core; by mass the stalk is roughly one fifth bast fiber and four fifths hurd. The long bast fibers are about 55 to 72% cellulose with about 2 to 5% lignin, together with hemicellulose, pectin and waxes. As in flax, the elementary fibers are polygonal plant cells with a lumen and show transverse dislocations (nodes), and they are cemented into technical bundles by pectin and hemicellulose. Reported fiber lengths and diameters vary widely with variety, retting and measurement method, so single values should be treated with caution.
hemp.process: Stems are cut and usually dew retted in the field, though water, enzymatic and other degumming methods are also used. Decortication then breaks the stem and separates fiber from hurd by breaking and scutching. For long-fiber yarns, the fiber is hackled and spun on flax-type long-fiber systems, often wet spun for finer counts. Alternatively, fiber can be cut and cottonized, using mechanical opening and sometimes chemical or enzymatic degumming, to lengths suited to short-staple cotton spinning and blending. Hurd is used separately for animal bedding, building materials and composites.
hemp.performance: Hemp shares many flax characteristics: high strength and stiffness, low elongation, ready moisture uptake and quick release, poor wrinkle recovery, charring rather than melting, and dyeability with cellulose dye classes such as reactive and vat dyes. Coarser, more lignified fiber gives a harsher hand and a slightly more yellowish tone, and fabrics usually soften with laundering. Cottonized hemp blended with cotton behaves much like cotton in handle and care. Claims of inherent antimicrobial, UV-blocking or thermal performance vary with fiber preparation and fabric construction and should be backed by test data for the specific product.
hemp.identify: Burn tests are indicative only and need fire precautions; hemp burns like other cellulose fibers, leaving soft gray ash. Under the microscope it looks much like flax, with nodes and cross markings, so separating the two is a known analytical difficulty. Laboratories combine methods such as the direction of twisting as a wet fiber dries, staining for lignin, and spectroscopy. In cottonized blends the hemp share is difficult to confirm by eye, so percentage claims rely on supplier documentation and quantitative analysis.
hemp.labeling: In the United States, hemp textiles are labeled with the fiber name and percentage by weight under the Textile Fiber Products Identification Act (15 U.S.C. 70 et seq.) and 16 CFR Part 303. THC limits govern cultivation, not garment labeling: the 2018 Farm Bill removed hemp at or below 0.3% delta-9 THC from the Controlled Substances Act definition of marijuana. In the EU, since 1 January 2023 the Common Agricultural Policy framework under Regulation (EU) 2021/2115 allows payments for approved hemp varieties with THC up to 0.3%, raised from 0.2%. EU labels follow Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011.
hemp.past: Hemp was long a cordage and heavy-cloth fiber. In the United States, the Marihuana Tax Act of 1937 burdened cannabis cultivation, including fiber hemp. During the Second World War, when imported cordage fibers were scarce, the US government produced the 1942 film Hemp for Victory to encourage farmers to grow hemp for rope and cordage, including for the Navy; after the war, cultivation declined again. Largely forgotten, the film resurfaced around 1989 in hemp advocacy. The 2018 Farm Bill separated hemp from marijuana in federal law, reopening commercial cultivation under state, tribal and USDA production plans.
facts: not more than 0.3% delta-9 THC, dry weight basis (7 U.S.C. 1639o)
roughly 20% bast fiber and 80% hurd by mass
